I have a little difficulty in finding answers to some of the following questions

1) How do i import my data making room for Multiple observer ( More than two observer group)

2) Will the use of DISTANCE Software alone sufficient for a PhD thesis in distance sampling research?

3) Is it possible to perform Bayesian Analysis in Distance? If not how can i perform posterior analysis in DISTANCE software or carry out Bayesian analysis with the results from DISTANCE?

Thanks to all and hope to get a maximum cooperation.

That’s interesting.  I did the Montrave analyses for the book using the Distance software interface.  I was not comfortable with estimation using the half-normal model.  In my analyses, AIC selected one HP adjustment narrowly over the half-normal model without adjustments, yet there was a warning of high correlation between parameter estimates for that model.  Usually in that circumstance, AIC would favour the simpler model.  The high correlation is no doubt what caused the convergence failure when you tried using the R package.  (It also explains the very poor precision for this model reported in the book.)  But it seems that you get a better AIC for the model without adjustments using the R package.  That suggests to me that the fit of the half-normal without adjustments when using the Distance interface has failed to converge, even though it reports that it did converge.

It is very rare for the half-normal model to have convergence problems of this type, but I suspect that this is the issue here, rather than you doing anything wrong.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Trapping Web Data
messages.body_plain:
Lauren:

Here is the contents of the 15 Sept 2005 message from Dr. Thomas regarding trapping web data.  We moved our email discussion list to Google-groups a couple of years ago.  I found the 15 Sept 2005 message on Google-groups, by simply entering "trapping webs" into the search box for this email list.  This is what I found:

"Each web is equivalent to a single point in a point transect design.  The sample effort is the number of trapping events.  Each trapped animal is equivalent to an observation in a point transect.  The distance of the trap
from the centre of the web is the distance to use for this "observation".

So, for example, say I had 1 stratum of area 100, containing 2 webs that I used for two trapping events (say trap nights).  I trapped 3 animals in the first (at distances 3, 5, 7) and 2 in the second (at distances 4, 5, 8) my
text file for data import might look like this:

area1 100 web1 2 3
area1 100 web1 2 5
area1 100 web1 2 7
area1 100 web2 2 4
area1 100 web2 2 5
area1 100 web2 2 8

Of course 2 webs is not enough to make reliable inferences about the stratum density, nor is 6 observations enough to reliably fit a detection function, but you get the idea. "

The short answer is trapping web data are equivalent (in data entry terms) to point transect data.  If you examine the projects: "Songbird.dst" or "Point Transect Example.dst" that ship as sample projects with Distance, that will provide guidance for your data input.

Hopefully that will get you started.

I can confirm that re-running the Montrave robin point count analysis repeatedly, the half-normal detection function, given an option to include Hermite adjustment terms, almost invariably chooses the half-normal with no adjustment terms.  Under that situation, the AIC is as you report, 444.78, and the estimate of robin density is 0.786 as reported in the online analysis report.

There are occasions where a 1 adjustment term Hermite is fitted to the robin data; none of my attempts resulted in an adjustment term model with a lower AIC than the no adjustment term model, as you report. Hi John:

Here's a simple example using the "minke" dataset provided in the
Distance R package, containing exact distances:

library(Distance)
data(minke)  # makes dataset available in workspace
#  next line sets the cutpoints between bins
#     read ds() documentation to note that the sequence
#     must include 0 and the maximum distance, number of bins=num.cutpts - 1
#       in your situation you would want seq(0,100,by=10)
cutpts <- seq(0, max(minke$distance, na.rm=TRUE), length=10)
#   having set the cutpoints, argument 'cutpoints' makes use of them
test <- ds(minke, cutpoints = cutpts)
plot(test)

library(Distance)

messages.body_plain:
To complement Eric´s answer.

The island has some 20km long, and the eucalyotus forest is patchy, but the patch distribution is heterogeneus.

Then, I would take in mind if there is connection of birds between patches, i.e. is it more frequent to find birds in neighbouring patches than in isolated patches?

Then I would stratify the island based on the amount of ecucalyptus forest/patches, and deploy point transects accodringly of the assumption that paradoltes live only in forest. Then you can apply much less effort to patches dominated by pastures.

Another option would be to move to Density Surface Models, but as fas as I know they are still not available in Distance for point transects...

Hi all, my name is Kevin Hawkshaw. I am an MSc student at the University of Alberta studying predator-prey interactions in Peregrine Falcons. I'm interested in trying to model prey abundance continuously through the course of the Peregrine breeding season. My daily or per transect sample sizes are in general not large enough to stratify my analysis that way, but i understand Distance has some other options like post-stratification and MCDS that may be solid alternatives. Can anyone offer some advice about what approach to take here? From some of the searching I have done it doesnt seem like anyone else has really attempted this before. Overall I have about 800 observations from 135 line transects, which are then broken down into 4 groups of prey. I have fit many global detection functions to those 4 groups so far using several different covariates, but I need to go from that to transect level or daily density estimates.

Thanks,
Kevin

We could use more information regarding your survey design.  Specifically, what is the level of spatial replication of your transects, and what is the temporal level of replication.  I'm guessing that the 135 transect to which you refer are something like 9 transects repeated 15 times or 5 transects repeated 27 times...

I ask because distance sampling has two levels of sample size: one (number of detections) for fitting the detection function and a second (number of spatial replicates) for assessing variability in encounter rate.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using line transect distance sampling on a large (8,000 ha) pasture to estimate bobwhite quail density response to grazing. We survey this area using 32 systematically placed lines (200 m apart) covering the entire pasture once a year in December. I have completed one year of this survey and am about to start the second survey out of ten more years. These first two years of survey represent density estimates pre-grazing and the remaining 8 years will be density in response to grazing.

My question is, should I keep these line transects permanent for the remaining years of the project or should I be changing their direction every year? We surveyed the lines East, West for the first year, is there any benefit to alternating between North,South and East,West each year?  If I had permanent transects, would I still have to pool detections over the years or is that only when a survey is repeated twice in a short time span? Thank you, I appreciate any advice, I am very new to survey design.
